instrucciones:
Recibes registros de una base de reglas de producción audiovisual con IA (texto completo, puede estar en
inglés, ruso o español). Para CADA registro devuelve:
- "enunciado": la regla en español, UNA frase, sin adornos: qué exige, prohíbe, limita o especifica. Si el registro
  es un ejemplo o una explicación sin norma, di qué ilustra ("Ejemplo: ...", "Explicación: ...").
- "alcance": a qué aplica exactamente (modelo y versión, caso T1-T5, etapa, tipo de pieza, régimen) o "general".
- "temas": de 1 a 3 claves de la lista, las que mejor describen de qué trata la regla.

[WhyStrohm. The Content Infrastructure Pitch › Brief] A 30-second founder explainer aimed at founders running content marketing themselves. The audience knows their content output is uneven and they're tired of the treadmill. The reframe is the WhyStrohm thesis: it's not a content problem, it's an infrastructure problem. The promise is the offer, 30 min/week of founder time, 48-hour cycle. The CTA is the free /scan diagnostic.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Brief] A 60-second founder explainer for WhyStrohm. The audience is operators and founders who already know they need a content system but haven't seen the WhyStrohm thesis articulated. The narrative arc moves through five micro-beats: hook, stakes, insight, proof, and CTA. Voice carries the explanation; on-screen text reinforces the key turns.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Beat framework: Founder Explainer] Five micro-beats:
0–2s. Hook (provocation); 2–14s. Stakes (why it matters); 14–32s. Insight (the actual point, extended for 60s to give the thesis room); 32–42s. Proof (the numbers); 42–60s. Insight wrap + CTA
[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Series lock] **Character anchor**: founder, mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, speaking directly to camera, calm authoritative posture
[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Series lock] **Environment**: minimalist home office, white walls, oak desk, single houseplant, late afternoon

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_01 · 0.0–2.0s · MCU · static] **Beat:** hook · **VO:** "Most founders treat content like a hobby."
**Subject:** founder, looking directly into camera, slight knowing smile, mid-statement.
**On-screen text:** "Most founders treat content like a hobby." (lower-third, hard-cut)
**Rationale:** Hook is provocative but calm, voice carries the bite. Direct eye contact, MCU lock-in.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_02 · 2.0–8.0s · MS · static] **Beat:** stakes · **VO:** "Then they wonder why every post feels like starting over. New idea, new angle, no compounding."
**Subject:** founder, gesturing slightly with one hand, explaining, eye contact maintained.
**Rationale:** Stakes beat. Pulled out to MS to let the gesture read. VO does the work, no on-screen text needed.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_03 · 8.0–14.0s · ECU · static] **Beat:** stakes · **VO:** "It's not creativity. It's missing infrastructure."
**Subject:** close on founder's eyes, considered expression, slight head tilt.
**On-screen text:** "It's missing infrastructure." (coral, lower-third, type-on)
**Rationale:** ECU pulls the audience into the realization moment. Text reinforces the line that needs to land.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_04 · 14.0–24.0s · MCU · push] **Beat:** insight · **VO:** "Every brand has a voice. Most founders never extract it. So every post starts from scratch."
**Subject:** founder, leaning slightly forward, more energy in delivery, hands resting on desk.
**Rationale:** Slow push as the thesis builds. VO is the load-bearing element here.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_05 · 24.0–32.0s · MS · static] **Beat:** insight · **VO:** "Extract it once. Lock it in code. Now every post compounds."
**Subject:** founder gestures toward laptop screen, kanban content pipeline, voice extraction interface, brand-lock file open in editor.
**On-screen text:** "Extract. Lock. Compound." (upper-third, slide-up)
**Rationale:** Show the artifact. Text reinforces the three-step pattern. Deep DOF keeps the screen legible.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_06 · 32.0–42.0s · MCU · static] **Beat:** proof · **VO:** "Hundreds of videos rendered from code. 48-hour content cycles. One operator."
**Subject:** founder, calm steady delivery, eye contact, hands folded.
**On-screen text:** "hundreds of videos · 48hr cycles · 1 operator" (upper-third, fade)
**Rationale:** Proof beat, concrete numbers. Stat callout lets viewer absorb visually while VO confirms.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_07 · 42.0–50.0s · MS · pull] **Beat:** insight · **VO:** "Not because we work harder. Because the system runs."
**Subject:** founder, slight smile, settled into the explanation, room visible around him.
**Rationale:** Slow pull releases tension. The thesis lands. VO carries, text would dilute.

[WhyStrohm. How The System Actually Works › Shots › shot_08 · 50.0–60.0s · MCU · static] **Beat:** cta · **VO:** "If this sounds like the version of content you actually want, run a free scan."
**Subject:** founder, calm, looks directly into camera one more time, almost-smile, settled.
**On-screen text:** "whystrohm.com/scan" (coral, lower-third, type-on)
**Rationale:** CTA beat. Static MCU brings it home. URL holds in lower-third for full read-twice duration.

[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Typography] Two-font stack for production. Mono only for technical content.
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Never list] - never use em dashes in copy (only periods, commas, semicolons)
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Never list] - never break the eye line between subject and the implied "operator perspective"

[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Color grade direction] Warm filmic, muted teal shadows. Slight grain. Cream highlights, deep navy/charcoal shadows, never crushed. Reminiscent of Kodak Portra 400 with a slight digital cleanup. Skin tones warm but not orange. Greens kept slightly desaturated to push focus to subject.

[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Motion language] Camera moves are minimal and deliberate. Default to static. When motion is used, slow push or slow pull only. Cuts on action, not on time. Type-on for emphasis, never bouncing or wobbling. Coral periods animate as a hard pop on signature beats. Transitions are hard cuts or 6-frame dissolves only, no fancy wipes, no zooms.

[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Motion language] For kinetic typography content (the Content Spiral pattern): pacing accelerates inward, each zoom 1.5–2x faster than the previous. Snap-back to wide claim is a hard cut.
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - no emojis in body copy
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - no exclamation points in headlines
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - no hype words ("game-changing", "revolutionary", "comprehensive", "next-level", "leverage")
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - no clichéd business metaphors ("move the needle", "drink the kool-aid", "low-hanging fruit")
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - no qualifiers in declarative copy ("perhaps", "maybe", "kind of")
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - prefer specific numbers over vague claims ("48 hours" not "fast", "30 minutes a week" not "a little time")
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - prefer present-tense over future-tense
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - prefer "operator" over "creator", "infrastructure" over "agency", "system" over "service"
[Brand Lock: WhyStrohm › Voice rules] - coral period (`.`) on signature lines is a typography choice, not punctuation, apply at end of hero phrases only

shot_05 still names seven adapters including Runway/Sora. Sora was discontinued and the
motion lane moved to Kling, Veo, Seedance, and Hailuo. The storyboard is deliberately left

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Brief] 90-second explainer for shotkit. Targets founder-led brands at $500K to $5M ARR who run their own content and feel the prompt-engineering tax. Walks through the diagnosis (vague brief plus model-roulette equals brand drift), the methodology (five-layer prompt anatomy), the build moment (brief in, files out), the proof (rendered preview from a real shotkit run), and the install command. Lives at the top of the shotkit blog post on whystrohm.com.
[shotkit. The Explainer. › Series lock] Field: **Character** · Value: No human subject. Typography-driven explainer with document-control aesthetic.
[shotkit. The Explainer. › Series lock] Field: **Environment** · Value: Operator-grade dashboard. Cream canvas, JetBrains Mono headers, Inter body, single coral accent per beat.
[shotkit. The Explainer. › Series lock] Field: **Lighting** · Value: Even diffuse. No shadow rolloff. Flat operator-doc grading throughout.
[shotkit. The Explainer. › Series lock] Field: **Color grade** · Value: Cream highlights (#F5F0E8), ink shadows (#2A2A32), coral (#D94F3A) reserved for signature beats. No saturation drift.

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Shots › shot_01: 0.0 to 12.0s. WS. eye-level. static.] **Beat:** pain. **Subject:** vague founder brief types into the left panel in JetBrains Mono. Cursor blinks. Then a chaos cut shows four image generators producing slightly off-brand outputs in a 2x2 grid. Each tile renders the same shot with a different palette, framing, font.
**On-screen text:** "You don't have a content problem. You have a pre-production problem." (Inter Black 900, center, fade)
**Rationale:** Cold open names the failure mode every founder recognizes. Vague brief plus model-roulette equals brand drift. The 2x2 grid does the work text cannot.

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Shots › shot_02: 12.0 to 30.0s. MS. eye-level. static.] **Beat:** reframe. **Subject:** Five horizontal layers stack from top to bottom. Each labeled in JetBrains Mono caps with 0.08em letter-spacing: brand lock, series lock, shot spec, text layer, generator adapter. Each layer slides in from below on a 6-frame stagger. Coral dot lands on brand lock as it appears.
**On-screen text:** "Five layers. Locked top to bottom." (Inter Black 900, upper-third, type-on)
**Rationale:** Architecture beat. The reader needs to see the layers exist before any claim about composability lands. Stack layout is the diagram doing the explanation.

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Shots › shot_03: 30.0 to 50.0s. MS. eye-level. push.] **Beat:** proof-1. **Subject:** Split panel. Left BRIEF column types out a brief slowly. Right OUTPUT column starts empty with a pulsing waiting dot, then file tree assembles row by row in JetBrains Mono Regular 16pt. storyboard.md, shots.json, text-overlays.json, brand-lock.snapshot.md, prompts/ directory with seven adapter files, preview.html. Coral dot lands on preview.html on completion.
**On-screen text:** "Brief in. Storyboard out. Audit trail included." (Inter Medium 500, upper-third, fade)
**Rationale:** The build moment is the centerpiece. Brief in, structured files out. Same animation language as the social demo so brand consistency reads across both surfaces.

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Shots › shot_04: 50.0 to 65.0s. MCU. eye-level. push.] **Beat:** proof-2. **Subject:** Coral wipe expands radially from the preview.html dot. Wipe reveals the rendered preview iframe scrolling vertically. The reader sees actual shot cards from the 30-second example pass through frame, including framing, angle, motion, color-grade rows. Subtle 10% vignette on edges.
**On-screen text:** "Files. Not panels. Not a SaaS dashboard." (Inter Black 900, lower-third, type-on)
**Rationale:** Reveal beat. The reader has now seen the methodology and the file outputs. The iframe shows the actual deliverable, not a mock.

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Shots › shot_05: 65.0 to 80.0s. MS. eye-level. static.] **Beat:** proof-3. **Subject:** Single shot description card sits center-frame. Seven generator adapter labels fan out radially around it. Midjourney, Flux, Ideogram, GPT Image, Nano Banana, Seedream, Runway/Sora. Lines connect center card to each adapter in 1px ink. Each adapter shows its prompt syntax appearing as a typewriter pass running simultaneously.
**On-screen text:** "One shot. Seven generators. One spec." (Inter Black 900, upper-third, fade)
**Rationale:** Cross-generator demonstration. Same shot description compiles to seven different prompt syntaxes simultaneously. The visual proves model-agnosticism is structural, not aspirational.

[shotkit. The Explainer. › Shots › shot_06: 80.0 to 90.0s. WS. eye-level. static.] **Beat:** promise. **Subject:** Full-frame typography. Install command appears via type-on in JetBrains Mono Regular at 22pt. Below it the project tagline in Inter italic 500 18pt, color muted. Coral period on the signature beat. Standard footer chrome holds.
**On-screen text:** "git clone github.com/whystrohm/shotkit / cd shotkit && ./install.sh" (JetBrains Mono, center, type-on) plus tagline "Pre-production for founder-led video at scale." (Inter italic 500, lower-third, fade).
**Rationale:** Promise beat. The viewer has the diagnosis, the architecture, the artifact, and the proof. The CTA is one paste-into-terminal command. No friction surface.

[Beat Frameworks] Pick one. Don't invent a new one unless the brief genuinely doesn't fit. Document the choice in `storyboard.md`.

[Beat Frameworks › Pain-Reframe-Promise (PRP)] Default for conversion content. Three beats:
1. **Pain**, name the audience's actual problem in their actual language. Concrete, not abstract. "Your content feels random" not "marketing inefficiency."
2. **Reframe**, flip the problem on its head. The point is *not* what they thought it was. "You don't have a content problem. You have an infrastructure problem."
3. **Promise**, what life looks like on the other side. Specific, verifiable, time-bound when possible.

[Beat Frameworks › Pain-Reframe-Promise (PRP)] Timing for 30s: 0–8 / 8–22 / 22–30.
Timing for 60s: 0–15 / 15–45 / 45–60.
[Beat Frameworks › Pain-Reframe-Promise (PRP)] Use when: ad creative, landing-page hero video, conversion-focused social.

[Beat Frameworks › Hero Trilogy] Default for product films and brand films. Three beats:
1. **World**, set the context. Who lives in this world. What's broken about it.
2. **Hero**, the product/founder/methodology arrives. Show what it does, not what it is.
3. **Transformation**, the world changes. Show before/after at scale.

[Beat Frameworks › Hero Trilogy] Timing for 60s: 0–20 / 20–40 / 40–60.
Timing for 90s: 0–30 / 30–60 / 60–90.
[Beat Frameworks › Hero Trilogy] Use when: product launches, brand films, anchor pieces.

[Beat Frameworks › Founder Explainer] Default for personal-brand video where a person speaks to camera. Five micro-beats:
1. **Hook**, a one-line provocation (0–2s)
2. **Stakes**, why this matters (2–8s)
3. **Insight**, the actual point (8–20s for 30s, 8–40s for 60s)
4. **Proof**, one concrete example or data point
5. **CTA**, what to do next, narrow and specific
[Beat Frameworks › Founder Explainer] Use when: founder content, thought leadership, personal-brand pieces.

[Beat Frameworks › Content Spiral] Default for kinetic typography or opinion content. The structure is recursive, each beat zooms in tighter:
**Wide claim**, the headline take; **Zoom 1**, one layer of nuance; **Zoom 2**, the layer underneath that; **Snap-back**, return to the wide claim, now reframed by the zooms
[Beat Frameworks › Content Spiral] Each zoom is 1.5–2x faster than the previous. Pacing accelerates inward.
[Beat Frameworks › Content Spiral] Use when: opinion videos, kinetic-type pieces, social-native commentary.

[Beat Frameworks › Educational Demo] Default for how-to content. Four beats:
**Problem state**, what someone is stuck on; **Reveal**, the technique or trick; **Walk-through**, apply it step by step; **Result**, the after-state, side-by-side with before
[Beat Frameworks › Educational Demo] Use when: tutorials, demo videos, training content.

[Beat Frameworks › Custom] If the brief doesn't fit, build a custom beat structure. Document in `storyboard.md`:
## Beat framework: Custom

**Why custom:** [one sentence, what made the standard frameworks insufficient]

**Beats:**
1. [name], [purpose], [duration]
2. ...
[Beat Frameworks › Custom] Custom is a last resort, not a first move. The standard frameworks exist because they work.
[On-Screen Text] Text on screen is a load-bearing decision. Most storyboards over-text. The default should be: **does this shot need text to land?** If the visual carries the meaning, text dilutes.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text earns its keep] 1. **Auto-play-mute environments.** Social feeds. Text replaces VO.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text earns its keep] 2. **Concept compression.** A short phrase lands harder than 4 seconds of narration.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text earns its keep] 3. **Stat or proof point.** Numbers stick visually in a way they don't audibly.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text earns its keep] 4. **Beat punctuation.** A single word or phrase that lands on a music hit.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text earns its keep] 5. **CTA.** The action you want the viewer to take.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text doesn't earn its keep] 1. **Restating the VO.** If the voice says it, the text is noise.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text doesn't earn its keep] 2. **Decorative copy.** "Moments matter" floating over b-roll. Cut it.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text doesn't earn its keep] 3. **Brand vibing.** Product names everywhere. Logo lockup in the CTA covers this.
[On-Screen Text › When on-screen text doesn't earn its keep] 4. **Filler beats.** If the shot doesn't need text, leave it clean.
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules] These flow into the `position` field of each text overlay.

[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Negative-space-aware composition] When a shot has on-screen text, the **shot subject must reserve space for it**. This is enforced at storyboard time, not generation time.

[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Negative-space-aware composition] If text is in the right third → subject composition leaves the right third clear.
If text is lower third → subject upper two-thirds.
If text is centered → subject framed to negative space around center.
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Negative-space-aware composition] This goes into the shot's rationale: "MCU left-third subject, reserves right-third for `text_03`."
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Positions] Position: `center` · Use when: Display headline, single concept, hard cut in/out
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Positions] Position: `lower-third` · Use when: Caption / VO substitute, persistent across shots
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Positions] Position: `upper-third` · Use when: Stat callout, secondary information
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Positions] Position: `left-third` · Use when: Subject is right-weighted in frame
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Positions] Position: `right-third` · Use when: Subject is left-weighted in frame
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Positions] Position: `{x: %, y: %}` · Use when: Custom, only when the standard positions don't fit
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Sizes] Size: `display` · Pixel approx (1080p): 96–144 px · Use for: Hero/hook beats
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Sizes] Size: `headline` · Pixel approx (1080p): 56–80 px · Use for: Reframe beats
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Sizes] Size: `body` · Pixel approx (1080p): 32–48 px · Use for: Caption-style, persistent
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Sizes] Size: `caption` · Pixel approx (1080p): 20–28 px · Use for: Disclaimers, attribution

[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Animation] Default to clean, not flashy:
- Hook beats → `hard-cut` in, `hard-cut` out (no fade)
- Reframe beats → `fade-in` 0.2s, `fade-out` 0.2s
- Persistent captions → `slide-up` in, `slide-down` out
- CTA → `type-on` for a typewriter effect, or `slide-up`
[On-Screen Text › Composition rules › Animation] Avoid stacking animations. Pick one per overlay.

[On-Screen Text › Color rules] The `color` field of every text overlay must be a hex value that exists in the brand-lock palette. If you find yourself wanting a color that's not in the palette, the answer is not to add it, the answer is to pick a different overlay style or shot composition.

[On-Screen Text › Typography rules] Same: every `font` field must reference a font defined in brand-lock typography. Two fonts max per project (display + body). More than that and the brand stops being recognizable.

[On-Screen Text › The "read twice" rule] Already covered in timing-rules.md but worth repeating: text needs to be on screen long enough for someone to read it twice. Calculate, then verify. Don't eyeball.

[On-Screen Text › Stacking text across shots] Text can persist across consecutive shots. This is useful when:
- The text takes longer to read than a single shot's duration
- You want text to feel anchored while visuals change underneath

[On-Screen Text › Stacking text across shots] To stack, both shots reference the same `on_screen_text` ID. The overlay's `enter.at` aligns to the first shot's start, `exit.at` aligns to the second shot's end.
[On-Screen Text › Stacking text across shots] Document this in rationale: "text persists across shot 3-4 to give 4.8s read-time for 16-word reframe."
[Shot Grammar] Controlled vocabulary. Use these exact terms in `shots.json`. Generators interpret loose language inconsistently, locked vocabulary survives translation.
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `ECU` · Name: Extreme close-up · What it shows: Eyes, hands, single detail
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `CU` · Name: Close-up · What it shows: Head, or full hand-on-object
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `MCU` · Name: Medium close-up · What it shows: Head and shoulders
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `MS` · Name: Medium shot · What it shows: Waist up
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `MLS` · Name: Medium long shot · What it shows: Full body, environment minimal
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `WS` · Name: Wide shot · What it shows: Full body, environment present
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Code: `EWS` · Name: Extreme wide shot · What it shows: Subject small in environment
[Shot Grammar › Framing (subject size in frame)] Default to MCU and MS for talking-head founder content. ECU and CU for product detail and emotion. WS and EWS for context-setting.
[Shot Grammar › Angle (camera vertical position)] Code: `eye-level` · Effect: Neutral, default
[Shot Grammar › Angle (camera vertical position)] Code: `high` · Effect: Subject feels smaller, vulnerable
[Shot Grammar › Angle (camera vertical position)] Code: `low` · Effect: Subject feels powerful, dominant
[Shot Grammar › Angle (camera vertical position)] Code: `overhead` · Effect: Detached, schematic, instructional
[Shot Grammar › Angle (camera vertical position)] Code: `dutch` · Effect: Tilted, tension, unease
[Shot Grammar › Angle (camera vertical position)] Default to eye-level. Use the others deliberately, not for variety.
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `static` · Effect: No movement · Use when: Default. Static is not boring.
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `push` · Effect: Camera moves toward subject · Use when: Building intensity, revealing
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `pull` · Effect: Camera moves away · Use when: Releasing, contextualizing
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `pan-left` / `pan-right` · Effect: Camera rotates horizontally · Use when: Surveying environment
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `tilt-up` / `tilt-down` · Effect: Camera rotates vertically · Use when: Reveal scale or detail
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `handheld` · Effect: Subtle organic shake · Use when: Documentary feel, urgency
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `orbit` · Effect: Camera circles subject · Use when: Hero shots, product reveal
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] Code: `whip` · Effect: Fast pan as transition · Use when: Beat-cuts in fast-paced content
[Shot Grammar › Motion (camera movement)] For AI-generated still frames, motion is mostly intent for the editor. For motion-video prompts (Kling, Veo, Seedance, Hailuo), motion translates directly.
[Shot Grammar › Depth of field] Code: `shallow` · Effect: Subject sharp, background blurred
[Shot Grammar › Depth of field] Code: `deep` · Effect: Everything in focus
[Shot Grammar › Depth of field] Code: `rack` · Effect: Focus shifts mid-shot
[Shot Grammar › Depth of field] Default to shallow for talking-head, deep for environmental and schematic.

[Shot Grammar › Lighting style (referenced from series_lock)] Don't redefine per shot. Define once in `series_lock.lighting`. Examples:
- `soft natural side-light, large window left, warm afternoon`
- `hard top-light, single source, deep shadows, studio black`
- `practical mixed sources, neon accents, urban night`
[Shot Grammar › Lighting style (referenced from series_lock)] The series_lock string flows into every prompt automatically.

[Shot Grammar › Subject description] Structured, not poetic. Pattern:
[who/what], [doing what], [emotional or compositional note]

[Shot Grammar › Subject description] Good:
"Founder, mid-thirties, leaning forward at laptop, face partially turned to window light"

[Shot Grammar › Subject description] Bad:
"A determined entrepreneur conquering the digital frontier with passion"
[Shot Grammar › Subject description] Generators reward precision. Adjectives describing emotion ("determined", "passionate") produce stock-photo aesthetics. Describe what the camera actually sees.

[Shot Grammar › What goes in `subject` vs `series_lock` vs `brand_lock`] This trips people up. The rule:
- **brand_lock**, locked across the entire project. Palette, type, "never" list.
- **series_lock**, locked across this storyboard. Character anchor, environment, lighting style, color grade.
- **subject (per shot)**, what's different about *this* shot. Action, expression, framing-specific composition notes.

[Shot Grammar › What goes in `subject` vs `series_lock` vs `brand_lock`] If you find yourself repeating the same lighting description across shots, it belongs in series_lock. If you find yourself repeating the same color description across storyboards, it belongs in brand_lock.
[Timing Rules] Pacing is math, not feel. Use these as defaults. Override only with reason documented in rationale.
[Timing Rules › Shot duration baselines] Content type: Kinetic typography / opinion · Default shot duration: 1.0–1.5s · Range: 0.5–2.0s
[Timing Rules › Shot duration baselines] Content type: Founder talking-head · Default shot duration: 2.5–4.0s · Range: 2.0–6.0s
[Timing Rules › Shot duration baselines] Content type: Product/lifestyle b-roll · Default shot duration: 1.5–2.5s · Range: 1.0–3.5s
[Timing Rules › Shot duration baselines] Content type: Demo / how-to · Default shot duration: 3.0–5.0s · Range: 2.0–7.0s
[Timing Rules › Shot duration baselines] Content type: Cinematic brand film · Default shot duration: 3.5–6.0s · Range: 2.0–10.0s
[Timing Rules › Shot duration baselines] If a single shot is longer than 7 seconds in a 30-second piece, justify it in rationale. Long shots are not bad. Unjustified long shots are.

[Timing Rules › Hook timing (the first beat)] The hook is 0–2s. Always. There are no exceptions in short-form content. Specifically:
- 9:16 social: first frame must telegraph the topic. Auto-play on mute means the first half-second is fighting a swipe.
- 16:9 in-feed: first 2s decides watch-time.
[Timing Rules › Hook timing (the first beat)] The hook shot framing should be high-contrast against the shots that follow. If shot 2 is MS, shot 1 should not be MS. Visual contrast = retention.

[Timing Rules › CTA timing (the final beat)] The CTA is the final 4–6s for 30s content, 6–10s for 60s content. Specifically:
- Last shot should hold long enough for someone to read the CTA text and act
- Don't put motion on the CTA shot, let the text breathe
- If there's a logo lockup, it lives in the final 2s, not earlier
[Timing Rules › On-screen text duration math] A text overlay needs to be on screen long enough to be **read twice**. Not once, twice. Why: viewers are skimming, eyes don't always lock on first frame.

[Timing Rules › On-screen text duration math] Reading speed reference (assume average viewer):
1 short word (≤5 chars): 0.6s minimum read; Short phrase (≤6 words): 1.2s; Sentence (≤14 words): 2.4s; Long sentence (15–25 words): 4.0s
[Timing Rules › On-screen text duration math] Multiply by 2 for the "read twice" rule. So a 6-word phrase needs **2.4s on screen minimum**.

[Timing Rules › On-screen text duration math] If a shot is 2 seconds and you need a 14-word sentence, you have a problem. Either:
1. Shorten the copy
2. Carry the text across two consecutive shots (text persists during cut)
3. Lengthen the shot
[Timing Rules › On-screen text duration math] Do not under-time text. It's the most common storyboard failure.

[Timing Rules › Pacing curve] For 30-second content, the natural energy curve:
0s ─────────────────────────────────── 30s

Energy
  ▲     ╱╲
  │    ╱  ╲___
  │   ╱       ╲___
  │  ╱            ╲___
  │ ╱                 ╲___
  └─────────────────────────►
   hook  build  apex  release  CTA
   0-2   2-12   12-20  20-26   26-30
[Timing Rules › Pacing curve] The apex is two-thirds in, not at the end. The CTA is a release, not a peak.
[Timing Rules › Pacing curve] For 60-second content, scale the same curve. Apex around 0:40, CTA from 0:50.

[Timing Rules › Validating timing] Before declaring done, check:
1. Sum of `(end - start)` across all shots equals project duration ±0.1s
2. No shot has `start >= end`
3. No two shots overlap
4. First shot starts at 0.0
5. Last shot ends at project duration
6. Every text overlay's `enter.at` is ≥ its shot's `start`
7. Every text overlay's `exit.at` is ≤ its shot's `end` (or carries to a flagged successor shot)
8. Every text overlay's on-screen duration ≥ read-twice threshold

[frontmatter › description] Render a structured storyboard (storyboard.md, shots.json, text-overlays.json, brand-lock.snapshot.md) into a single-file HTML preview that is shareable, printable, and offline. Use when the user wants to share a storyboard, export for review, hand off to an editor, or print a hard copy. Triggers on "preview the storyboard", "share this", "export to HTML", "print version", or after a storyboard-architect run. Produces one self-contained .html file with no build or server.

[Storyboard HTML Preview] You are turning structured storyboard files into a single shareable HTML document. The output is what an editor, stakeholder, or client opens in a browser without thinking about it.

[Storyboard HTML Preview] The constraint is non-negotiable: **single file, no build step, no server, works offline.** Any time the output requires "run this build command" or "host this somewhere," the skill has failed.

[Storyboard HTML Preview › When to use] Trigger when the user:
- Asks to preview, share, or export a storyboard
- Wants a printable version
- Says "what's the next step" after a storyboard-architect run
- Hands off `storyboard.md` + `shots.json` + asks for a deliverable for review

[Storyboard HTML Preview › What you produce] One file: `preview.html`. Self-contained. Inline CSS. No JavaScript dependencies (vanilla JS only, embedded). No external font files (uses system stack with brand-font fallbacks). No external images (placeholder slots; if generated images exist, embed as base64 OR reference relative paths).

[Storyboard HTML Preview › What you produce] output/
├── run.json                   # input, for the run id and date
├── storyboard.md              # input
├── shots.json                 # input
├── text-overlays.json         # input
├── brand-lock.snapshot.md     # input
├── frames/round-N/            # input, if generation has happened
├── critiques/round-N/         # input, for the verdict badges
└── preview.html               # ← what this skill produces

[Storyboard HTML Preview › What you produce] If the user has generated frames, the HTML references them via relative paths so the file
works when the whole `output/` folder is shared. Resolve a shot's frame in this order:
An entry in `shot.assets.generated` marked `accepted: true`; The newest entry in `shot.assets.generated`; `frames/round-{highest}/{shot_id}.{png,jpg,jpeg,webp}`; `generated/{shot_id}.{ext}`, the pre-3.0.0 flat layout

[Storyboard HTML Preview › What you produce] Data first, convention second. Reading the path convention first meant the page showed
whatever file happened to sit there, accepted or rejected, first draft or fifth re-roll.

[Storyboard HTML Preview › What you produce] If no frames exist yet, the HTML uses styled placeholder cards with the shot spec, still
useful for review and handoff.
